prompt: You are about to make a right turn from a two-way street. Where should your vehicle be as you approach the corner?
choices: Close to the right curb or edge of the road
Near the center line, so you have room to swing around the corner
In the middle of the lane, away from the curb
Partly in the lane to your left
explanation: Approach a right turn as far to the right as practical, close to the curb or road edge. Swinging toward the center line first makes your intent unclear and leaves room on your right for others.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 24, AZ p. 47, NJ p. 74)

prompt: You turn right from one two-way street onto another that has two lanes in your direction. Unless signs or markings say otherwise, which lane should you end the turn in?
choices: The left lane, so you are out of the way of parked cars
Whichever lane is empty at the moment
The lane closest to the right curb or edge
The lane next to the center line
explanation: Begin and end a right turn in the lane closest to the right edge of the road. Do not turn wide into another lane; change lanes later if you need to.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 27, NY p. 36, AZ p. 47)

prompt: Why is it a mistake to swing out to the left just before you make a right turn?
choices: It wears out your tires faster
It leaves a gap on your right that a car, bicycle, or motorcycle can move into
It forces you to turn into the far lane of the new street
It is only a mistake when the road is wet
explanation: Keeping close to the right curb before a right turn reduces the chance that another road user ends up in the space on your right as you turn. A wide swing also confuses drivers behind you.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 74, NH p. 31, AZ p. 47)

prompt: Just before you turn right, what extra check should you make?
choices: Look in your left side mirror for passing cars
Tap the horn to warn anyone nearby
Glance at the speedometer
Check your right mirror and look over your right shoulder for bicyclists or pedestrians next to you
explanation: Bicyclists, motorcyclists, and pedestrians can be between your vehicle and the curb, often in your blind spot. Check the right mirror and over your right shoulder before turning.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 24, NY p. 36)

prompt: You turn right onto a two-way street with two lanes in your direction, and you plan to turn left one block later. What should you do?
choices: Turn directly into the left lane to save time
Turn into the right lane, then signal and change lanes when it is safe
Turn into the right lane and stay there, then turn left from it
Stop in the intersection until the left lane is clear
explanation: Finish a right turn in the right lane, then signal, check your blind spot, and move over when safe. Turning straight into a far lane can put you in the path of other turning traffic.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 36, AZ p. 47, TX p. 46)

prompt: When you make a right turn, what path do your rear wheels follow compared with your front wheels?
choices: A shorter path, closer to the curb
Exactly the same path
A wider path, farther from the curb
A path that depends only on your speed
explanation: A turning vehicle's rear wheels track inside the front wheels, so on a right turn they pass closer to the curb. Leave enough room so your rear wheel does not hit the curb or people waiting at the corner.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 36, CA p. 49, AR p. 76)

prompt: On a two-way street with no left-turn lane, where should you position your vehicle to turn left?
choices: As close as possible to the right curb
In the lane or part of the lane just to the right of the center line
Straddling the center line
In the oncoming lane, so you are ready to turn
explanation: Approach a left turn from the part of your side of the road closest to the center line. Never cross into oncoming lanes before you actually turn.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 47, NY p. 37, CA p. 25)

prompt: A street has a marked left-turn lane at the intersection ahead. Where should you make your left turn from?
choices: From the lane next to the turn lane, if it is less crowded
From any lane, as long as you signal
From the marked left-turn lane
From the right lane after the light turns green
explanation: When a lane is signed or marked for left turns, use that lane. Turning left from another lane cuts across drivers who are going straight.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 47, CA p. 25, TX p. 37)

prompt: You turn left from a two-way street onto another two-way street. Which lane should you end the turn in?
choices: The lane just to the right of the center line
The lane closest to the right curb
The center left-turn lane, if there is one
Whichever lane lets you take the widest, smoothest turn
explanation: End a left turn in the left-most lane going your way, just to the right of the center line. This avoids conflict with oncoming drivers turning right onto the same street.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 27, NY p. 37, AZ p. 47, NJ p. 75)

prompt: You want to turn left from a one-way street onto a two-way street. Which lane should you turn from?
choices: The right lane
The center lane
Any lane, as long as you signal
The far-left lane
explanation: When turning left from a one-way street, start from the lane nearest the left curb, then turn into the lane just right of the center line of the two-way street.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 27, AZ p. 47, NY p. 36)

prompt: You turn left from a two-way street onto a one-way street that has two lanes. Which lane should you end in?
choices: The right lane of the one-way street
The left lane of the one-way street
Either lane, whichever you can reach by turning wide
The lane that matches the side of the road you came from
explanation: Approach from the lane closest to the center of the two-way street and turn into the left lane of the one-way street. Change lanes afterward if needed.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 47, NY p. 37, CA p. 27)

prompt: You turn left from a one-way street onto another one-way street. Both have two lanes. Which lanes should you use?
choices: Start in the right lane and end in the right lane
Start in the right lane and end in the left lane
Start in the left lane and end in the left lane
Start in the left lane and end in the right lane
explanation: On a left turn from one one-way street onto another, start in the far-left lane and finish in the left lane of the street you enter.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 36, NJ p. 75, AZ p. 47)

prompt: You turn left from a two-lane road onto a four-lane highway (two lanes each way). Which lane should you enter first?
choices: The lane closest to the right shoulder
The oncoming lane nearest the center
Whichever lane is open, by crossing both lanes at once
The lane just to the right of the center line, moving right later when it is safe
explanation: Turn into the lane nearest the center line on your side of the highway. When traffic permits, signal and move to the right lane.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 75, NY p. 37, AL p. 23)

prompt: You and an oncoming driver are both waiting to turn left at the same intersection. When it is safe, how should you each turn?
choices: Each turns to the left of the center of the intersection, so your paths do not cross
Each drives past the center of the intersection before turning
One driver waits until the other has fully cleared the intersection
Each swings wide to the outside lanes of the new street
explanation: Opposing left-turning drivers should each turn before reaching the center point, passing in front of each other. Driving past the center would make your paths cross.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 75, PA p. 53, AZ p. 47)

prompt: While you are stopped, waiting to turn left, how should your front wheels be pointed?
choices: Turned slightly left, so you are ready to go
Straight ahead
Turned slightly right, toward the curb
It does not matter while you are stopped
explanation: Keep your wheels straight until you actually begin the turn. If they are turned left and you are hit from behind, you could be pushed into oncoming traffic.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 25, NY p. 34, CO p. 16)

prompt: You are waiting to turn left. An oncoming car has its right turn signal on. What should you do?
choices: Turn now, because the car is clearly turning right
Flash your headlights to tell the driver to turn
Turn quickly before the car reaches the intersection
Wait until the car actually starts its turn before you go
explanation: A turn signal shows intent, not action. The driver may have left it on by mistake or may be turning just past you, so wait until the vehicle begins to turn.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 30)

prompt: Why should you look especially carefully for oncoming motorcycles before turning left?
choices: Motorcycles always have the right-of-way
They are small and hard to see, and their speed and distance are hard to judge
Motorcycles cannot stop on wet pavement
Motorcyclists usually do not use headlights
explanation: Many crashes happen when a driver turning left fails to see an oncoming motorcycle or misjudges how fast it is coming. Look twice and wait if you are unsure.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 35, NY p. 37)

prompt: You are turning left across two lanes of oncoming traffic. A driver in the nearer lane stops and waves you on. What should you do?
choices: Go immediately, since the driver is letting you through
Wave back and turn slowly through both lanes
Make sure the far lane is also clear before you turn, because the stopped car may hide traffic
Honk to warn the far lane, then turn
explanation: Never start a left turn until you can see that every lane you must cross is clear. A stopped car can block your view of a vehicle coming in the next lane.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 53, CO p. 16)

prompt: What makes a left turn "protected"?
choices: Oncoming traffic is stopped by a signal while you turn
There is a center median on the street you are entering
You are turning from a marked left-turn lane
No pedestrians are in the area
explanation: During a protected turn, such as on a green arrow, the signal holds oncoming traffic so your turn path is clear of it. You still watch for anyone who is already in the intersection.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 40, AL p. 57)

prompt: You are turning left onto a divided highway that has a wide median. How should you make the turn?
choices: Turn left into the first roadway you reach
Cross the first roadway, then turn left into the far roadway on the other side of the median
Turn left and drive in the median until there is a gap
Turn right first, then make a U-turn across the median anywhere
explanation: A divided highway is like two one-way roads. Cross the near roadway when traffic from the left is clear, then turn left beyond the median when traffic from the right is clear. Turning left too early puts you into oncoming traffic.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 53)

prompt: Before you move into a center two-way left-turn lane, what hazard should you check for?
choices: Parked cars along the curb
Drivers coming toward you who are also using the center lane
Bicyclists in the right lane
Vehicles waiting at the next stop sign
explanation: Drivers from both directions share the center lane, so look ahead for oncoming vehicles already in it before you enter.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 22, AZ p. 48)

prompt: How should you enter a center two-way left-turn lane to turn left?
choices: Signal, check your blind spot, and move completely into the center lane
Stay half in your lane so you can return quickly
Stop in your travel lane first, then angle into the center lane
Enter it as early as possible to get out of traffic
explanation: Signal, check over your shoulder, and merge completely into the center lane so you do not block traffic behind you. Then turn when it is safe.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 22, AZ p. 48)

prompt: Why should you enter a center two-way left-turn lane only shortly before your turn, instead of driving in it for a long stretch?
choices: Driving in it longer uses more fuel
It is only for vehicles larger than cars
It is not a travel lane, and the farther you drive in it, the more likely you are to meet a driver turning from the other direction
It is reserved for buses between intersections
explanation: The center lane exists so you can slow and wait for your turn. Using it as a travel lane is not allowed and greatly raises the risk of a head-on conflict with oncoming turners.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 37, CA p. 22, AZ p. 48)

prompt: When should you move into the correct lane for an upcoming turn?
choices: Right at the intersection
Only after you start to turn
Only when the traffic light turns green
Well before the turn, and sooner when traffic is moving faster
explanation: Plan ahead and get into the proper lane well before the turn. The faster traffic is moving, the earlier you should change lanes.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 45, AL p. 23, PA p. 52)

prompt: When may you turn from a lane other than the one closest to the direction you are turning?
choices: Whenever traffic is light
Only when signs or pavement markings show that turns are allowed from that lane
Whenever you signal early enough
Only at night
explanation: Normally you turn from the lane closest to the direction you are going. Some intersections allow turns from more than one lane, and signs, signals, or pavement arrows will show it.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 27, AZ p. 47, CO p. 15, AL p. 23)

prompt: You are in one of two side-by-side left-turn lanes. What should you do during the turn?
choices: Stay in your own lane from start to finish
Move into the other lane if it looks smoother
Speed up to get ahead of the car turning next to you
Cut the corner to finish the turn faster
explanation: With double turn lanes, another driver is turning right next to you. Pick your lane before the turn and stay in it until the turn is complete.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NH p. 31, PA p. 52, NJ p. 58)

prompt: You turn left from the right-hand lane of two left-turn lanes. Where should you end the turn?
choices: In the lane nearest the center line
In the matching lane, which is the second lane from the center line, following any guide lines
In any lane, since both lanes are turning
In the lane farthest right, ready for parking
explanation: With dual turn lanes, each lane turns into its matching lane on the new street. Follow the painted guide lines through the intersection so you do not cross into the other turning car's path.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NE p. 64, CO p. 15, PA p. 52)

prompt: While turning in one of two side-by-side turn lanes, what extra danger should you watch for?
choices: Vehicles behind you changing lanes
The traffic light changing to green
The vehicle turning next to you drifting into your lane
Pedestrians on the far side of the street you just left
explanation: In dual turn lanes, the driver beside you may stray into your turning path. Stay centered in your lane and keep an eye on the car next to you.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 52)

prompt: You realize you are in a lane marked with a turn-only arrow, but you wanted to go straight. What should you do?
choices: Go straight, since you have not started turning yet
Stop and wait for a gap to move into the next lane
Make the turn the lane requires, then find another route
Turn on your hazard lights and go straight
explanation: Lane-use arrows are mandatory. If you are in a turn-only lane, you must turn. Then find a safe, legal way back to your route.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 52, TX p. 37)

prompt: Heavy traffic keeps you from reaching the turn lane for your street. What is the safest choice?
choices: Cut across the lanes at the last moment
Stop in your lane and wait for a gap, even if traffic behind you must stop
Turn from the wrong lane while signaling
Pass this turn and take the next safe route or turn around later
explanation: If you cannot get into the proper lane in time, do not turn. Keep going and turn at the next opportunity; last-second lane changes cause many crashes.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 45, CA p. 21)

prompt: Halfway through a left turn, you realize it is the wrong street. What should you do?
choices: Stop in the intersection and back up
Finish the turn, then find a safe place to turn around
Swerve back into your original lane
Stop and wait for traffic to clear before reversing
explanation: Once you start a turn, follow through. Stopping or backing up in an intersection is dangerous; complete the turn and correct your route later.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 21, NH p. 31)

prompt: What is the main purpose of using your turn signal before a turn?
choices: To ask other drivers for permission to turn
To let other drivers, bicyclists, and pedestrians know what you plan to do
To give you the right-of-way
To make your car more visible at night
explanation: A signal communicates your intentions so others can react. It does not give you any special right to turn.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 15, AZ p. 26)

prompt: You have just finished a turn. What should you check about your turn signal?
choices: That it is still on, so drivers know you just turned
That it has switched to the hazard flashers
That it is off, so others do not think you are turning again
Nothing, since signals always cancel themselves
explanation: Make sure your signal is canceled after the turn. A signal left on can mislead other drivers into pulling out in front of you.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 74, AL p. 23, NH p. 31)

prompt: When should you turn on your signal for a turn?
choices: Early enough that other road users can see it and react before you slow and turn
After you start steering into the turn
Only if another car is directly behind you
Only when you are already stopped at the corner
explanation: Signal before you begin to slow and turn, so drivers and pedestrians have time to react. The exact minimum distance is set by your state.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 46, CA p. 24, CO p. 15)

prompt: Before you pull into an intersection from a stop, in what order should you look?
choices: Left, right, then left again
Right, left, then right again
Straight ahead only
Left only, then go
explanation: Use the left-right-left scan. Look left first, then right, then left again before you pull out.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 24, PA p. 42, NY p. 34)

prompt: Why do you look to the left first, and then left again, before entering an intersection?
choices: Drivers from the left always have the right-of-way
Traffic from the left is in the nearest lane and reaches you first
Your car's blind spot is always on the left
Signs are posted on the left side of the road
explanation: Vehicles coming from the left are closest to you. A final look left catches a car you may have missed the first time.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 42, CA p. 24)

prompt: Besides traffic, what should you check before turning at an intersection?
choices: Only the traffic light
Whether the car behind you has its lights on
The crosswalks on your left and right for people about to cross
Only the street you are leaving
explanation: Search all corners and crosswalks before you turn. Pedestrians in the crosswalk of the street you are entering are easy to miss.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 35, NH p. 31, AZ p. 47)

prompt: Where should you look while you are making a turn?
choices: At the curb right next to your front tire
At your hands on the steering wheel
In the rearview mirror
Through the turn, toward the far end of the path you will follow
explanation: Look through the turn to the farthest point you can see along your path. This helps you steer smoothly and spot hazards early.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NH p. 31)

prompt: You must stop at an intersection that has a painted stop line. Where should you stop?
choices: With your front bumper over the line
Behind the stop line
In the crosswalk, past the line
At the edge of the cross street
explanation: When there is a stop line, stop before your front bumper reaches it. Stopping over it can put you in pedestrians' path.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 24, PA p. 14, CO p. 10)

prompt: You must stop at an intersection with no stop line and no crosswalk. Where should you stop?
choices: Before entering the intersection, at a point where you can see approaching traffic
In the middle of the intersection
One car length past the corner
Anywhere, since there is no line
explanation: With no stop line or crosswalk, stop before entering the intersection, at the point nearest the cross street where you can see traffic coming.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 10, CA p. 24)

prompt: You stopped correctly at the stop line, but parked trucks block your view of the cross street. What should you do?
choices: Go, because you already stopped
Honk and drive through quickly
Back up to get a wider view
Check for pedestrians, then creep forward slowly until you can see clearly
explanation: After the required stop, yield to pedestrians and edge forward carefully until you can see. Then go only when the way is clear.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 14, CO p. 10)

prompt: Your light is green, but traffic is backed up on the far side of the intersection. What should you do?
choices: Enter the intersection and wait there
Stay behind the line until there is room for your vehicle on the far side
Pull halfway into the crosswalk
Go around the stopped traffic on the shoulder
explanation: Do not enter an intersection unless you can get all the way through. Stopping inside it blocks cross traffic when the light changes.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 30, NY p. 35, CO p. 16)

prompt: Traffic is crawling, and you are about to stop across the entrance of a side street. What should you do?
choices: Stop where traffic stops, even across the side street
Pull onto the shoulder
Turn on your hazard lights so side-street drivers wait
Stop before the side street so you leave it open
explanation: Watch for cross streets and offset intersections in slow traffic. Leaving them open prevents gridlock.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 35)

prompt: Why do trucks and buses often swing wide when they turn?
choices: Their drivers cannot see the curb
Their brakes work better on wide turns
Their rear wheels follow a shorter path than the front wheels
They are required to use two lanes
explanation: When any vehicle turns, the rear wheels cut inside the path of the front wheels. The longer the vehicle, the bigger the difference, so large vehicles swing wide to keep the rear wheels off the curb.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 49, AR p. 76, CO p. 23)

prompt: A large truck ahead of you has its right signal on but moves left before the corner, leaving space on its right. What should you do?
choices: Stay behind the truck and let it finish its turn
Pass on the right through the open space
Honk so the driver stays in the lane
Pull alongside on the left
explanation: Trucks swing left to make tight right turns. If you move into the gap on the right, you can be caught between the truck and the curb.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 57, AK p. 83, NV p. 63)

prompt: You are stopped at a red light. A large truck on the cross street signals to turn into your street and seems to have little room. What should you do?
choices: Pull forward over the stop line to get out of its way
Stay stopped behind the stop line and leave the truck room to complete its turn
Edge forward so the truck driver can see you clearly
Honk to warn the truck driver that you are there
explanation: Large vehicles need extra space to turn and may swing into nearby lanes. Stay stopped behind the line (do not pull into the intersection) and give them room.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AK p. 83, CA p. 49, CO p. 23)

prompt: In the United States, which way does traffic travel around a roundabout?
choices: Clockwise
Either direction, depending on your exit
Toward the nearest exit, in either direction
Counterclockwise
explanation: Traffic moves counterclockwise around the central island. You always enter by turning right and keep the island on your left.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 46, NY p. 50, TX p. 56, PA p. 54)

prompt: You want to go to the exit on the left side of a roundabout. How do you enter?
choices: Turn right into the roundabout and circle around to your exit
Turn left into the roundabout to take the shortest path
Drive across the central island
Enter in whichever direction has less traffic
explanation: Never turn left to enter a roundabout. Enter to the right of the central island and travel counterclockwise until you reach your exit.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AL p. 60, AZ p. 28, CA p. 46)

prompt: What should you do first as you approach a roundabout?
choices: Speed up to merge with circulating traffic
Slow down and watch for pedestrians at the crosswalk
Turn on your left signal
Move to the far-right lane, whatever your exit
explanation: Roundabouts are designed for low speeds. Slow down as you approach and be ready to stop for pedestrians in the crosswalk before the entry.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 46, PA p. 54, NY p. 50)

prompt: You miss your exit in a roundabout. What should you do?
choices: Stop and back up to the exit
Stop and wait for traffic to let you over
Exit across the central island
Keep going around until you come back to your exit
explanation: If you miss your exit, continue around the roundabout again. Never stop or back up in a roundabout.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 46, AL p. 60, AZ p. 28)

prompt: Which turn signal should you use as you approach your exit from a roundabout?
choices: Right turn signal
Left turn signal
Hazard flashers
No signal, since the road curves
explanation: Signal right as you near your exit so drivers waiting to enter and pedestrians know you are leaving the circle.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 51, PA p. 54, TX p. 56, NE p. 57)

prompt: At a two-lane roundabout, you plan to take the first exit to the right. Unless signs show otherwise, which lane should you use?
choices: The left lane
The right lane
Either lane, then cut across at the exit
The truck apron
explanation: To turn right in a multi-lane roundabout, enter in the right lane and exit in the right lane. Always follow lane signs and pavement arrows.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 46, NV p. 44, NE p. 57)

prompt: At a two-lane roundabout, you plan to turn left (go about three-quarters of the way around). Unless signs show otherwise, which lane should you use?
choices: The right lane
The lane with the shortest line
The left lane
The right lane, then move left inside the circle
explanation: For a left turn or U-turn at a two-lane roundabout, use the left lane, as shown by signs and pavement arrows.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NV p. 44, NE p. 57, CA p. 46)

prompt: When should you choose your lane at a multi-lane roundabout?
choices: After you enter the circle
Only when you reach your exit
Whenever a gap opens in the circle
Before you enter, based on your exit and the lane signs and markings
explanation: Read the lane-use signs and pavement arrows as you approach and pick your lane before entering. Do not wait until you are in the circle.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 56, NY p. 50, NE p. 57)

prompt: A tractor-trailer is entering a roundabout next to you. What should you do?
choices: Stay out of its way and do not drive beside it or pass it
Drive next to it so it can see you
Speed up to get ahead of it in the circle
Follow it closely onto the truck apron
explanation: Large vehicles may need more than one lane in a roundabout. Give them room and do not try to pass or ride alongside them.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 56, AZ p. 28, NE p. 57)

prompt: What is the raised, paved area next to the central island of some roundabouts for?
choices: Cars that want a shortcut to their exit
Parking for emergency vehicles
The rear wheels of large trucks that need extra room to turn
Bicyclists who do not want to ride in traffic
explanation: A truck apron gives the rear wheels of long vehicles room as they turn. Cars, pickups, and SUVs should not drive on it.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AL p. 60, NE p. 57, NV p. 44)

prompt: A bicyclist is riding in the travel lane inside a single-lane roundabout ahead of you. What should you do?
choices: Pass the bicyclist inside the circle
Stay behind the bicyclist and do not pass in the roundabout
Honk so the bicyclist moves to the edge
Use the truck apron to go around
explanation: Bicyclists may ride through a roundabout like any vehicle. Do not pass them inside the circle; stay behind until you both exit.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 50, PA p. 54, CA p. 46)

prompt: A line of cars is waiting at a roundabout entry, and the car ahead of you is stopped at the yield line. Where should you wait?
choices: In the crosswalk, as close as possible to the car ahead
Behind the crosswalk, keeping it clear for pedestrians
Inside the circle, next to the waiting car
On the truck apron
explanation: When you are not first in line, do not stop in the crosswalk. Keep it clear so pedestrians can cross.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 50)

prompt: Once you are inside a roundabout, when should you stop?
choices: Only when necessary to avoid a crash or other danger
At every entry point, in case cars are waiting
Whenever you need time to read the exit signs
Halfway around, to check your mirrors
explanation: Traffic in the circle should keep moving. Stopping without need can cause a rear-end crash; if you are unsure of your exit, just go around again.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AL p. 60, AZ p. 28, CA p. 46)

prompt: Where is a U-turn most dangerous?
choices: On a quiet residential street with a clear view
Near the top of a hill or on a curve
At a wide intersection with no traffic
In an empty parking lot
explanation: Near a hilltop or curve, other drivers cannot see you in time to stop. Do not make a U-turn anywhere your view, or other drivers' view of you, is limited.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 37, NV p. 46, MT p. 49)

prompt: You see a NO U-TURN sign at an intersection, and no cars are coming. May you make a U-turn there?
choices: Yes, if there is no traffic
Yes, if you use the left-turn lane
Yes, if you signal first
